name: Xylometazoline

lead: Xylometazoline is an over-the-counter nasal spray that shrinks swollen nasal tissue so breathing is easier. It has been sold since 1959.
People interested in facial redness note that it works by vasoconstriction, but its labeled use is nasal congestion.

paras: It activates alpha-adrenergic receptors on nasal blood vessels, narrowing them and reducing swelling.

Irritation, headache and nosebleed are reported. Use beyond about five to seven days is not advised because of rebound congestion. Check with a clinician if pregnant or if you have high blood pressure or heart conditions.

chain: Constricts blood vessels in the nasal lining
Clearer airway; vasoconstriction is also the property behind interest in redness
angle.text: The nasal spray relieves congestion by shrinking nasal vessels, which makes nose breathing easier. People interested in redness reduction point to the same vasoconstrictor action, though the labelled use is congestion and no trial has tested it for facial redness.

lead: Xylometazoline is an over-the-counter imidazoline nasal decongestant sold as sprays and drops under names such as Otrivin, Otrivine and Otriven.[1] It narrows the blood vessels of the nasal lining, which reduces swelling and opens the airway for easier breathing through the nose.[2]

Its appearance relevance runs through the nose and face. Clear nasal breathing is tied to how people carry their mouth and jaw, and decongestants are used in clinics around rhinoplasty airflow testing, where xylometazoline has been applied during breathing measurements before and after surgery.[3] Some people interested in facial redness point to the same vasoconstrictor action, although the nasal product itself is labelled for congestion.[4]

The drug was patented in 1956 and entered medical use in 1959. It is on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List and is available as a generic.[1] Trials have examined it for congestion, nosebleed prevention during intubation, sleep apnea with congestion, bronchoscopy and other settings.[5][6][7]

paras: Xylometazoline has no labelled cosmetic indication. In appearance-minded circles it comes up for nasal breathing, and by extension for how the nose and midface function, and for temporary vasoconstriction of visibly flushed skin. A 2021 randomised trial of rhinoplasty technique measured nasal airflow before surgery and six months afterwards, with and without xylometazoline, to separate lining swelling from structure; its reported group comparisons were about osteotomy technique, not about the drug.[3]

Labelled use is temporary relief of nasal congestion from colds, hay fever and sinusitis.[1] Clinics also use nasal decongestants before nasal procedures, such as in endoscopy and intubation.[5][7][8] The US label advises asking a doctor if symptoms last over 7 days.[4]

Xylometazoline is a direct alpha-adrenergic agonist that acts on receptors in nasal blood vessels, causing local vasoconstriction.[2][9] It is an imidazole derivative designed to mimic adrenaline, and one cited study describes it as a highly selective alpha-2A agonist.[1][9]
Wikipedia lists an elimination half-life of about 10 to 12 hours with excretion in urine. The hydrochloride salt is the form used in medicines.[1]

Nosebleed prevention: a randomised trial in children found that xylometazoline with lidocaine jelly reduced nosebleeds after nasotracheal intubation (7.5% versus 27.5% with saline).[5] A 2024 randomised trial compared cocaine with xylometazoline for the same purpose.[10]
Sleep apnea: a crossover trial in twelve people with sleep apnea and nasal congestion tested a week of xylometazoline against placebo.[6]

Bronchoscopy: a randomised, double-blind trial of 148 patients undergoing flexible bronchoscopy compared 0.1% xylometazoline with saline spray. Operators rated ease of scope passage the same in both groups, and facial pain, nasal pain and mucosal trauma did not differ; the authors concluded their findings did not support its use for this purpose.[7]

Infants: a retrospective cohort of 898 hospitalised infants under two years found adverse events in 10.5 per 100 episodes with xylometazoline plus saline versus 20.0 per 100 with saline alone; no definite drug-linked life-threatening events were identified, and three nosebleeds were probably linked to the drug.[11]
Ear function: a nonrandomised study found that nasal decongestants usually did not change eustachian tube opening, and a minority of patients showed reduced function.[12]
Common cold: a Cochrane review examined nasal decongestants as monotherapy for the common cold.[13] A 2026 review found no rebound congestion in studies of up to 10 days of xylometazoline use.[14]
No published trial of xylometazoline for facial redness or rosacea was found.

Reported effects include nasal irritation, headache, nosebleed, nausea and trouble sleeping.[1] Because it is sympathomimetic, labelling advises against use in people with high blood pressure or heart problems and it is not recommended in pregnancy.[1]

Long use beyond about five days is not recommended, because stopping can cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) and tolerance can develop.[1] A 2026 review found no rebound congestion in studies of up to 10 days.[14] A case series on addiction to nasal decongestants is cited by Wikipedia.[1] A 2021 FDA communication noted a proposed child-resistant packaging rule for imidazoline decongestants.[1]

Otrivin is the most widely used international name, with Otrivine in the UK and Otriven in Germany. Xylometazoline is sold over the counter in the UK and the US.[1] Otrivin Oxy, a related product, contains oxymetazoline instead.[1]

Xylometazoline appears occasionally in T Nation forum posts. A 2001 thread titled Otrivin noted that its active ingredient is xylometazoline and that a poster understood sports bodies restrict it.[15] Posters in another thread discussed a nasal product containing it while comparing over-the-counter availability of decongestants across countries.[16]
